name: Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher waitlist
list_status: closed to new applicants; opened by lottery June 3 to 9, 2024 (online), paper postmark deadline June 28, 2024; first opening since Dec. 10, 2009

figures.spread_note: Point count at list creation; NYCHA has not published the current remaining count.

source.title: NYCHA Establishes New Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Waitlist and Begins Notifying Applicants of Lottery Results
source.quote: 200,000 households were randomly selected for the waitlist via lottery

figures.grade_reason: Agency press release with date; not structured data; current remaining count not published.
caveats: Count at creation, not today. The release says only that 'applicant eligibility must be confirmed'; how households leave the list is not described in the source.

The release uses several words for the same 200,000: 'households' and 'applications' in the body, 'New Yorkers' and 'families and individuals' in quotations. The registry records households, following the sentence that describes the list, and flags the inconsistency.

People who remained on the pre-2024 list 'will continue to be served and did not have to reapply', so the total list at creation exceeded 200,000; the Mayor's Management Report monthly count (nycha-section8-waitlist-mmr) was 203,000 in July 2024, peaked at 205,000 in August 2024 and stood at 197,000 in June 2025.
One household may also be on the public housing list and in Housing Connect lotteries.

figures.period_label: Online applications June 3 to June 9, 2024; paper applications postmarked by June 28, 2024

source.title: NYCHA Establishes New Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Waitlist and Begins Notifying Applicants of Lottery Results
source.quote: In total, NYCHA received 633,808 online applications during the eligible window, including 301,044 within the first 24 hours. Households could also request a paper application; NYCHA received 4,416 paper applications that were postmarked by the June 28 deadline.

caveats: Applications, not households: the release counts 633,808 online and 4,416 paper applications and separately says 200,000 were selected.

figures.spread_note: 2023 actual was 7,538 vouchers for the year, about 628 a month (release: 'Last year, NYCHA issued 7,538 vouchers').
figures.period_label: Stated goal, Aug. 1, 2024, for 'the next several years'

source.title: NYCHA Establishes New Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Waitlist and Begins Notifying Applicants of Lottery Results
source.quote: NYCHA will utilize and call households off this waitlist over the next several years, with a goal of issuing 1,000 vouchers a month contingent on funding and the authorized voucher capacity.

figures.grade_reason: A goal, not a measured rate; the 2023 actual is measured.
caveats: A goal 'contingent on funding and the authorized voucher capacity', in the release's words; not a measured rate.
NYCHA testified Sept. 29, 2025 that issuance to the general waitlist was temporarily paused to absorb Emergency Housing Voucher households.
The 7,538 figure for 2023 is in a separate sentence: 'Last year, NYCHA issued 7,538 vouchers'.

figures.spread_note: 200,000 / 12,000 a year = 16.7 years at the stated goal; 200,000 / 7,538 = 26.5 years at the 2023 pace.
figures.grade_reason: Derived; assumes list worked in order, no attrition, constant throughput. All three assumptions are false in practice.
caveats: Shown only as an illustration of scale, never in totals.

raise_grade: FOIL to NYCHA for current waitlist count by household size and borough preference, and vouchers issued per month since Aug. 2024.

name: Food vendor waiting list (Department of Health)
what_for: A mobile food vending permit or license: the source says 'licenses'; DOHMH's rule governs the 'full-term permit waiting list'. The registry keeps both words until the agency clarifies.
list_status: open in periods set by rule (last application period deadline April 28, 2026)

figures.period_label: On or before Dec. 18, 2025 (date of report; agency date not given)

source.title: Thousands more NYC street vendors will be able to operate legally under new Council bill
source.publisher: Gothamist (Arya Sundaram), attributing the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
source.quote: The Department of Health said 5,236 people are on the waitlist for food vendor licenses.

figures.grade_reason: Press report attributing the agency; no agency date; the article says 'licenses' where the rule says 'permits'.
caveats: The Gothamist source says 'waitlist for food vendor licenses'; the DOHMH rule (effective Dec. 12, 2021) creates a 'full-term permit waiting list' with up to 445 permits a year for 10 years from July 1, 2022. Which list the 5,236 refers to is not stated.
The Dec. 18, 2025 source describes a Council bill, later Local Law 54 of 2026 per the DCWP proposed rule; the enacted text has not been captured here.

raise_grade: FOIL to DOHMH for waiting list count by date, position ordering rule and permits issued per year since 2022.

name: Buildings filings (DOB NOW): filing to approval, computed distribution
what_for: Approval of a construction job filing

figures.spread_note: Computed by this project from every DOB NOW job filing with an approved_date in the window, in fractional calendar days. The single median blends two populations: professionally certified filings (median about 1.6 days) and standard plan examination (median about 27 days, 90th percentile about 150). The mean (36.5) is five times the median.

source.title: DOB NOW: Build – Job Application Filings
source.publisher: Department of Buildings via NYC Open Data

figures.definition_quote: filing_date: date the job filing was submitted. approved_date: date the filing was approved (dataset field names; DOB's data dictionary should be quoted here once retrieved).
figures.grade_reason: Computed from record-level public data with the query published; reconciles against the Mayor's Management Report average (dob-filing-to-approval).
caveats: Only filings that reached approval are in the window; filings still pending are not counted, so this is a completed-wait figure.
Approval is plan approval, not permit issuance or sign-off.
Negative durations (none found) would be excluded.
filing_date carries no time of day, so durations are computed from midnight; a date-only computation gives a median of 6.0 and 90th percentile of 89.

raise_grade: Already re-queryable. Add the still-pending filings as a waiting-so-far figure.

name: Housing complaint problems: received to closed, computed distribution
what_for: Resolution of a housing maintenance complaint
unit: items (problems; one complaint can carry several problems)

figures.spread_note: Computed by this project. Non-emergency problems: median 12.7 days, 90th percentile 81.8; in Manhattan the 90th percentile is 107 days, in Staten Island 27.

source.title: Housing Maintenance Code Complaints and Problems
source.publisher: Department of Housing Preservation and Development via NYC Open Data
source.quote: fields received_date and problem_status_date, problem_status = CLOSE, problem_duplicate_flag != Y

figures.grade_reason: Computed from record-level public data with the query published; reconciles against HPD's Mayor's Management Report medians (hpd-close-emergency, hpd-close-nonemergency).
caveats: 'Closed' is HPD's status, not a repair: it includes no-access, not-found and tenant-withdrawn outcomes.
Problems still open are not in the window (completed-wait figure).
37,659 rows flagged as duplicates were dropped before computing (blind recount).
Durations use full timestamps; 105 problems were received before 2025, one in 2013, and are included.

raise_grade: Quote HPD's data dictionary for status_description categories; add open problems as waiting-so-far.

name: Civil service eligible lists
what_for: Appointment to a permanent civil service job from a ranked list
end_event: Appointment, or the list's expiry; lists are established for one to four years and can be extended
list_status: rolling (lists established as exams are scored)

figures.spread_note: Distribution across 850 lists and 428 titles is in the source project's data; a person can appear on more than one list.

source.title: How New York City hires (methodology and data)
source.publisher: Josh Greenman, computed from DCAS Civil Service List (Active), vx8i-nprf

figures.definition_quote: Stock: Civil Service List (Active), vx8i-nprf (source project methodology).
figures.grade_reason: Computed from a re-queryable DCAS dataset; entries not deduplicated to persons.
caveats: List entries, not unique people: one person can be on several lists.
Many on a list hold other jobs; being on a list is a formal ask (an exam taken and passed) but not always an active wait.
Live count on Sept. 5, 2026 was 403,777 rows, 855 exams, 432 titles (blind recount); the registry keeps the dated July 13, 2026 figure.

Lists are often extended past four years: on Sept. 5, 2026, 92,636 of 403,777 rows carried an extension date beyond their anniversary and 88,082 entries sat on lists past the four-year mark (example: Conductor exam 6601, established Feb. 14, 2018, extended to Feb. 14, 2027). Blind recount, live data.

raise_grade: Deduplicate to persons (names are in the dataset) and compute time-on-list distribution by title.

name: Housing Connect: verification and approval (Furman Center sample)
what_for: Approval for an affordable lottery unit

figures.spread_note: Furman reports medians by stage and the funnel shares; it notes 'many applicants face significantly longer times' without publishing percentiles.
figures.period_label: Furman Center sample; the report does not state the sample's date range (report published April 2026)

source.title: The House Doesn't Always Win: Understanding NYC's Housing Connect Lottery System and How to Improve It
source.quote: the median time to complete the verification and offering process and be approved is 118 days

figures.definition_quote: Median Time from receiving a log number and median time from document review to decision (Figure 5 caption).
figures.grade_reason: Independent research center report from a sample of marketing-agent records; not re-queryable.
caveats: A sample of lotteries drawn from marketing-agent processing records; the report warns its sample may overestimate processing times. Not all lotteries.
HPD's own fiscal 2025 median of 142 days runs from certificate of occupancy to approval (see hpd-lottery-applicant-approval), a different span.
Excludes, per the report, the time for appeals, complaints, HPD's audit of files and lease signing.
figures.what_for: Approval for an affordable lottery unit, measured from receipt of a log number

figures.unit_of_value: unique applicants ('nearly 600,000', HPD estimate cited by Furman)
figures.spread_note: Applications per building range from about 1,000 to more than 40,000 (Furman citing HPD). The 600,000 unique-applicant estimate is undated; the six million applications are for 2024.
figures.period_label: Undated HPD estimate cited by the Furman Center (report published April 2026)

source.title: The House Doesn't Always Win
source.quote: estimated nearly 600,000 unique Housing Connect applicants

figures.grade_reason: Research report citing HPD; the six million is applications and the 600,000 is Furman's estimate of unique applicants.
caveats: Two units from two periods: six million applications (2024) and roughly 600,000 unique applicants (undated HPD estimate). The registry does not compute a ratio between them.

name: 3-K applicants placed in a program they did not list
what_for: A seat in one of the 3-K programs the family listed
end_event: Offer to a listed program (from the waitlist over the summer) or acceptance of the assigned program
list_status: annual application round; waitlists per program

figures.spread_note: Every applicant received an offer, per the source; the 6,000 received a program they had not listed and were waitlisted for their listed choices. District variation in filled seats is from an Independent Budget Office report cited in the article.
figures.period_label: 3-K offers for the 2025-26 school year, released May 20, 2025

source.title: NYC's preschool offers leave waitlists in some districts, empty seats in others
source.publisher: Chalkbeat New York (Michael Elsen-Rooney), citing Education Department officials
source.quote: Roughly 15% of 3-K applicants, more than 6,000 students, didn't get into any of the programs they listed on their application

figures.grade_reason: Press report attributing Education Department officials; no primary document captured.
caveats: Prior round (offers April 2024): more than 2,400 children left without seats out of 43,000 applicants (CBS New York, May 16, 2024).

For 2026-27 the city said every on-time applicant would receive an offer (Chalkbeat, Jan. 30, 2026); 94,840 3-K and pre-K applications in 2025. Chalkbeat's 'more than 27,000 of roughly 136,000 seats' unfilled is for 'the city's free child care programs for children ages 4 and under', a wider set than 3-K and pre-K alone.

raise_grade: Education Department offer-round data by district (FOIL or Council testimony).

name: Trees and Sidewalks repair program
what_for: City repair of a sidewalk damaged by a street tree, for owner-occupied one- to three-family homes
end_event: Repair completed (the 419-day figure covers repaired sidewalks only); other outcomes are waitlisting or a referral to hire a contractor
unit: items (the 419-day mean is over 1,069 repaired sidewalks; the 101-day mean is over service requests)
list_status: open; sites rated 1 to 100, only the highest rated repaired

figures.standard: 30-day internal service level for inspection after a request (audit: missed by 71 days on average); no target time frame for inspection-to-repair (audit)
figures.spread_note: Audit gives two means with different denominators: 101 days request-to-inspection (all inspected requests) and 419 days inspection-to-repair (repaired sidewalks only), plus tail shares and the maximum; no median.
figures.period_label: Audit scope July 1, 2015 through Dec. 31, 2017 (report: 'The scope of this audit was July 1, 2015 through December 31, 2017'); the 419-day mean covers 1,069 sidewalks repaired in fiscal 2017, July 1, 2016 to June 30, 2017

source.title: Audit Report on the Department of Parks and Recreation's Trees & Sidewalks Program (MH18-058A)
source.quote: our review of 1,069 repaired sidewalks found that the average time from inspection to repair was 419 days, with the longest time for a repair taking over 11 years.

figures.definition_quote: Site has been waitlisted: This site meets the criteria for repair. However due to a high number of requests we are only able to repair the very highest rated sites at this time. (Parks program page, retrieved Sept. 5, 2026)
figures.grade_reason: Oversight audit with dates; seven years old; no current count of waitlisted sites is published.
caveats: Stale: repairs from fiscal 2017. The program page (2026) still shows a waitlist tier for sites rated 80-90 and a three-year expectation for 90-100.
Eligibility is limited to owner-occupied Tax Class 1 homes; everyone else is told to hire a contractor, which is a rationing rule, not a queue.

raise_grade: FOIL to Parks for the count of sites in 'Inspected - Site Waitlisted' status by borough and year of inspection, and repairs completed per year.

name: Housing Court active eviction cases
what_for: Resolution of an eviction case (both parties wait)

figures.spread_note: No distribution of case age published in the source.
figures.period_label: March 2020 to March 2024 per the report's key findings (the report's introduction instead dates the rise from the January 2021 end of the eviction moratorium; the registry uses the dated version)

source.title: Evictions Up, Representation Down: How New York City is Undermining the Right to Counsel
source.quote: Between March 2020 and March 2024, the number of active eviction cases in New York rose 440%, from approximately 33,000 cases to 177,000 cases.

figures.definition_quote: Data from the New York State Office of Court Administration via the OCA Data Collective (report footnote 6); 'active eviction cases' is not further defined in the report.
figures.grade_reason: Oversight report with a stated data source and period; the report gives two different start points for the same rise; 'active' undefined.
caveats: Tier 3: state courts. Never in city totals.
The figure is as of March 2024, more than a year before the report and two and a half years before this registry.
Both landlords and tenants are in this line; it is a docket, not an application queue.

The report's introduction dates the rise from the January 2021 end of the moratorium; its body says the moratorium 'expired on January 15, 2022'; the key findings give March 2020 to March 2024. The registry uses the dated key-findings version.

raise_grade: Pull current pending-case counts from the Office of Court Administration or the Housing Data Coalition, with 'active' defined.
